s01: A small cloud spreads,
although no particle knows which way to go.
Here is a simple model of diffusion.
Each dot takes an equal step,

choosing up, down, left,
or right at random.
The choices are independent.
Some paths wander back.
Others reach farther.
The cloud has no preferred direction,
but its spread still grows.
There is a gentle surprise in that growth.
To double the typical distance from the start,
we need four times as many steps.
Let us see why.
To define the spread,
square the distance from the start
and average across all possible walks.
That expected value increases
by one squared step every turn.
A tiny example makes the cancellation visible.
Begin two steps to the right.
The squared distance is four.

The next step can leave
squared distances
of nine, one, five, or five.
Their average is five: exactly one more.
In general, opposite steps cancel
the terms that depend on direction.
Only one squared step remains.
After sixteen steps, the mean squared distance is sixteen.
Taking its square root gives a spread of four steps.
After sixty four steps, the spread is eight.
Four times the time, twice the spread.
This is a root mean square distance,
not a boundary containing every particle.
Flowing water can also carry the whole cloud;
that is a different motion.
Even directionless wandering has a mathematical rhythm.
